props.title: The War on Democracy
props.initialSlug: The truth is the ultimate weapon.

sections.content: **The War on Democracy** (2007) marks a pivotal moment in political documentary filmmaking, with veteran journalist John Pilger exposing the dark underbelly of US intervention in Latin America. The film powerfully parallels similar hard-hitting documentaries like **The Revolution Will Not Be Televised** (2003) and **South of the Border** (2009), using firsthand accounts and declassified documents to reveal covert operations. Pilger's direct interviews with Hugo Chavez and ordinary citizens create an intimate portrait of Venezuela's struggle, while archiving crucial historical moments like Chile's 1973 coup against Salvador Allende.

sections.content: The film's examination of media manipulation connects strongly to later works like **All the President's Men** (1976) and **Spotlight** (2015), showing how investigative journalism can expose government deception. Pilger's approach influenced a wave of political documentaries including **Dirty Wars** (2013) and **The Panama Deception** (1992), establishing a template for combining historical analysis with contemporary investigation.

What sets **The War on Democracy** (2007) apart is its grassroots perspective, interviewing indigenous activists and local organizers rather than just political figures. This bottom-up approach influenced later works like **Even the Rain** (2010) and **También la Lluvia** (2010), which examine Latin American resistance through both historical and contemporary lenses. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Political Documentary

The film's lasting influence can be seen in works like **Citizenfour** (2014) and **The Act of Killing** (2012), which similarly combine investigative journalism with powerful personal testimonies. Pilger's direct confrontation of US foreign policy opened doors for filmmakers like Jeremy Scahill and Laura Poitras to pursue equally challenging investigations of power structures.
